theme: Individual responsibility; elegy for Israel’s princes [survey]
readingInstruction: Read Ezekiel 18:1-20:49. This is a survey day. Chapter 18 is the great chapter on individual responsibility and God’s desire for repentance. Chapter 19 is a lament for Israel’s princes. Chapter 20 is another review of Israel’s history. Focus on chapter 18.
settingTheScene: The exiles had a proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.” They were blaming their ancestors for the exile and saying that nothing they did could change it. God answers through Ezekiel with one of the most important chapters on personal responsibility and repentance. Chapters 19 and 20 then give two more views of Israel’s story: laments for her kings and another review of her history of rebellion.
observation: “What do you mean by repeating this proverb… The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge?” (18:2).
“Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins shall die” (18:4).
“If a man is righteous and does what is just and right… he shall surely live, declares the Lord GOD” (18:5, 9).
“Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (18:23).
“Yet you say, The way of the Lord is not just. Hear now, O house of Israel: Is my way not just?” (18:25).
“Repent and turn from all your transgressions, lest iniquity be your ruin” (18:30).
“Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?” (18:31).
“For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live” (18:32).
interpretation:
The proverb about sour grapes expresses fatalism. The exiles felt trapped by their ancestors’ sins. God rejects the proverb and states a principle: each person is accountable for their own sin. “The soul who sins shall die.” The chapter gives three cases: a righteous father who lives, his violent son who dies, and his righteous grandson who lives. The grandson does not die for the father’s sins. Each stands on his own.

The point is not that God abandoned the principle of corporate solidarity, which appears elsewhere. It is that no one can blame the past to avoid responsibility. And it is also a word of hope: a wicked person who turns from sin will live. “None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him.” Repentance is real. The way is open.

The question God asks in verse 23 is among the most beautiful in the Bible: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked… and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” God does not enjoy judgment. His desire is that people turn and live. The exiles complain that “the way of the Lord is not just,” but God replies that his ways are just. It is their ways that are unjust.

The chapter ends with an invitation: “Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit!” It sounds like a command to do the impossible, since later chapters will promise that God himself gives the new heart (36:26). Both are true. We are commanded to turn, and God enables the turning. “For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone; so turn, and live.” The gospel is already audible.

Chapter 19 is a dirge about Judah’s last kings, as lion cubs trapped and a vine uprooted. Chapter 20 reviews God’s mercy and Israel’s rebellion from Egypt, closing with a promise to gather them and be sanctified in them.
connection: 2 Peter 3:9 says that the Lord is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” 1 Timothy 2:4 says he desires all people to be saved. Romans 14:12 says that each of us will give an account of himself to God. John 9:2-3 shows Jesus rejecting the idea that suffering always traces to a particular person’s sin. Acts 3:19 calls us to repent. Romans 6:23: “The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life.”
application:
Ask whether you are using someone else’s sin or your past as an excuse. Take responsibility, and then turn to God.

Write down Ezekiel 18:32 and carry it with you as a reminder of God’s heart.

Offer the invitation of this chapter to someone who feels trapped: “Turn, and live.”
prayerPrompts: Confess where you blame others or your past.
Turn from a specific transgression and tell him so.
Thank him that he has no pleasure in anyone’s death.
